claim: Aged mice (20-22 months old) produce shorter action sequences compared to young mice (2 months old) during instrumental learning.
source: We found that, after extended training, aged mice produced shorter actions and displayed squeezed automatic behaviours characterised by ultrafast oligomeric action chunks that correlated with deficient reorganisation of corticostriatal activity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Both young and aged mice significantly escalated their overall lever press rate as the ratio requirement increased during training.
source: Throughout training, both young and aged mice significantly escalated their overall performance (LP rate) as the ratio requirement to obtain an outcome increased (mixed ANOVA using factors of training and age F(3.5,48.9) = 116.852, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis with specific F-values and p-values is provided to support this claim.

claim: Overall instrumental performance was equal in young and aged mice during training.
source: A non-significant training x age interaction (F(3.5,48.9) = 1.153, p=0.341) suggested that overall instrumental performance was equal in young and aged mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing non-significant interaction and reference to supporting figure.

claim: Aged mice produced a larger number of action sequences per minute halfway through training compared to young mice.
source: However, half way through this training, aged mice produced a larger number of action sequences per minute, whereas young mice stabilised, or diminished, their sequence rates (Figure 1C). This was supported by a significant effect of training (F(16,224)= 28.885, p<0.001) and a significant training x age interaction (F(16,224) = 3.716, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis with specific F-values and p-values, plus reference to Figure 1C showing the data.

claim: Both young and aged mice were able to extend the number of execution elements in their sequences throughout training.
source: Further, a comparison of action sequences between days 7 and 17 of training revealed that both young and aged mice were able to extend the number of execution elements in their sequences throughout training (F(1,14) = 158.282, p<0.001) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Aged mice extended their sequences to a lesser extent than young mice.
source: This increase was of a different magnitude (as suggested by a significant day x age interaction (F(1,14) = 40.03, p<0.001)), indicating that aged mice extended their sequences to a lesser extent than young mice.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant interaction effect.

claim: Young mice showed significant increases in sequence duration from day 7 to day 17, but aged mice did not.
source: In contrast, analysis of sequence duration showed a significant day x age interaction (F(1,14) = 8.368, p<0.05) with significant increases of sequence duration in young (F(1,7) = 18.376, p<0.01) but not aged (F(1,7) = 1.745, p=0.228) mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values for both groups, plus reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Aged mice displayed a marked increase in the number of sequences that broke through the sequence trigger.
source: Importantly, aged mice showed evidence of learning about the ST applied from day 10, as they displayed a marked increase in the number of sequences that broke through the ST and therefore frequently accessed the RR schedule (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Observation supported by reference to figure showing the data.

claim: Young mice comfortably incorporated the sequence trigger requirement.
source: In contrast, young mice kept these numbers low, suggesting that they comfortably incorporated the ST requirement (F(3.065,42.908) = 7.757, p<0.001; training x age interaction F(3.065,42.908) = 6.027, p<0.01) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Statistical analysis and reference to supporting figure.

claim: The delivery of pellets in operant conditioning boxes generated a clear vibration signal that was more salient than the sound of the dispenser engagement and/or pellet dropping.
source: First, we confirmed that the delivery of pellets in the operant conditioning boxes generated a clear vibration signal, which was more salient than the sound of the dispenser engagement and/or pellet dropping (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Direct observation confirmed by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing the measurements.

claim: All mice reduced their reaction time between pellet delivery and first magazine check as magazine training progressed.
source: We found that all mice reduced their reaction time between pellet delivery and first magazine check (first check intervals) as training progressed (mixed ANOVA with factors training and age F(5,70) = 25.822, p<0.001), indicating that they learned to detect when pellets were delivered.
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values supporting the observation.

claim: The reduction in reaction time between pellet delivery and magazine check was similar in both young and aged groups.
source: A non-significant training x age interaction (F(5,70) = 0.360, p=0.874) confirmed that this reduction was similar in both groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and D).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing non-significant interaction, plus reference to supporting figures.

claim: Both young and aged mice showed a similar increase in magazine approach responses throughout magazine training.
source: This similar performance was not due to a higher overall number of magazine checks in the aged group, since both young and aged mice showed a similar increase of magazine approach responses throughout this training (F(5,70) = 25.822, p<0.001; training x age interaction F(5,70) = 0.360, p=0.874) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to supporting figure.

claim: Both young and aged groups displayed parallel escalations of lever hold times up to approximately 0.5 seconds.
source: In this task, both young and aged groups displayed parallel escalations of LH times up to ~0.5 s.
evidence: Direct observation from the lever hold task data.

claim: Young mice increased their lever hold times throughout subsequent stages of training, whereas aged mice maintained their maximum performance around 0.5 seconds.
source: However, young mice increased their LH times throughout subsequent stages of training, whereas aged mice maintained their maximum performance around 0.5 s holds (Figure 2C).
evidence: Observation supported by reference to Figure 2C showing the data.

claim: The time of lever hold significantly varied as instrumental training progressed in both age groups.
source: Statistical analysis supported this observation: mixed ANOVA (factors: training and age) showed that the time of lever hold significantly varied as instrumental training progressed in both age groups (F(16,176) = 73.471, p<0.001), although there was a significant training x age interaction, indicating that the age of the animals significantly affected their performance (F(16,176) = 16.796, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values.

claim: Both young and aged groups independently elevated their lever hold performance throughout training despite differences between groups.
source: Importantly, simple effects analyses confirmed that despite these differences, both groups independently elevated their performance throughout training (Young: F(16,112) = 69.387, p<0.001; Aged: F(16,64) = 51.33, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis with separate F-values and p-values for each group.

claim: Only young mice managed to produce sustained lever presses that approached or exceeded each lever hold requirement.
source: Event scatter plots at different LH requirements revealed that, although both groups displayed a large number of very short presses, only young mice managed to produce sustained presses that approached, or exceeded, each LH requirement (Figure 2D).
evidence: Observation from event scatter plots shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Aged mice produced a much higher proportion of very short inter-press-intervals compared to young mice.
source: However, subsequent analysis of the serial response times based on inter-press-intervals (IPIs) recorded on the same day revealed that aged mice produced a much higher proportion of very short IPIs (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that they were reaching a higher sequence speed than young mice.
evidence: Analysis of IPI data shown in referenced figures.

claim: Aged mice displayed spates of lever presses with over 13 presses per second, much faster than the fastest bursts recorded in young mice.
source: We found a strikingly high speed of responding in aged mice, in some instances displaying spates of LP with over 13 presses per second, much faster than the fastest bursts recorded in young mice (Figure 3C, Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: Acoustic data analysis shown in Figure 3C and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The speeds of lever pressing in aged mice are similar to fully automatised scratch reflex movements in mice.
source: These speeds are similar to fully automatised scratch reflex movements in mice (Inagaki et al., 2003).
evidence: Comparison to published data on scratch reflex movements.

claim: Average speed within fast bursts was significantly higher in aged than young mice.
source: Quantification analysis of fast sequences confirmed that average speed within fast bursts (in number of presses/sec) was significantly higher in aged than young mice (t(7.417) = −4.201, p<0.01, Figure 3D), whereas within-burst IPIs were significantly shorter (t(14) = 2.724, p<0.05, Figure 3E).
evidence: Statistical analysis with t-values and p-values, plus reference to supporting figures.

claim: Despite their speed of responding, aged mice were less efficient at earning rewards.
source: Interestingly, despite their speed of responding, aged mice were less efficient at earning rewards (t(14) = 3.101, p<0.01), indicating that although their action bursts often broke through the sequence trigger (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), they rarely completed the RR requirements (Figure 3F).
evidence: Statistical analysis with t-value and p-value, plus reference to supporting figures.

claim: Both young and aged mice similarly reduced within-sequence inter-press-intervals throughout training.
source: In both young and aged mice, within-sequence IPIs (Figure 3G, blue) clustered around a similar interval space (from ~0.1 to ~1 s intervals) by day 13, suggesting that both groups developed chunking of within-sequence (i.e. execution) elements. In support of this, we found that both young and aged mice similarly reduced the within-sequence IPIs throughout training (Figure 3H), as reflected by a significant effect of training (two-way mixed ANOVA with factors training and age: F(1.955,27.377) = 18.606, p<0.001) but no training x age interaction (F(1.955,27.377) = 0.562, p=0.573).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to supporting figures.

claim: The variability of within-sequence inter-press-intervals was equally reduced in both young and aged groups.
source: Similarly, the variability of these IPIs was equally reduced in both groups (Figure 3H, inset), again showing a significant effect of training (F(2.352,32.904) = 6.545, p=0.003) with no training x age interaction (F(2.352,32.904) = 1.785, p=0.179).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to supporting figure.

claim: Young mice displayed longer sequence boundary intervals that were distant from the chunking space, whereas aged mice accumulated them in a narrow band near the chunking space.
source: On the other hand, the development of sequence boundary intervals throughout training (Figure 3G, orange) was very different in young and aged mice. Whereas young mice displayed longer boundary intervals that were distant from the chunking space, aged mice tended to accumulate them in a narrow band near the chunking space (Figure 3G).
evidence: Observation from Figure 3G showing the distribution of sequence boundary intervals.

claim: The narrow band of sequence boundary intervals appeared earlier in training (day 10) in all aged animals, before within-sequence intervals chunked.
source: Importantly, this band appeared earlier in training (day 10) in all aged animals, before within-sequence intervals chunked (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Observation from figures showing temporal progression of chunking patterns.

claim: Young mice showed an increase in sequence boundary intervals from days 10 to 17, whereas aged mice kept these intervals consistently low.
source: This was evidenced in the quantitative analysis, where the young group showed an increase in sequence boundary intervals from days 10 to 17, whereas the aged group kept these intervals consistently low (Figure 3I), as indicated by a significant effect of training (F(3.884,54.375) = 8.005, p<0.001) and a significant training x age interaction (F(3.884,54.375) = 4.729, p=0.003).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to Figure 3I.

claim: Aged mice displayed lower variability in sequence boundary intervals than young mice from day 10 to 17.
source: Although no drop in variability for this interval was found from day 10 to 17 (F(7,98) = 1.428, p=0.203), aged mice displayed lower variability than young mice in this period (F(1,14) = 8.855, p=0.01) (Figure 3I, inset), suggesting that the temporal relationships of boundary elements in aged mice had already been established in day 10 (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to supporting figures.

claim: There was a significant age x region interaction in neuronal activation across cortical and striatal regions.
source: Two-way ANOVA (factors: age; region) revealed no overall effect of age (F(1, 111)=1.868, p=0.174), although there was a significant age x region interaction (F(7,111) = 2.136, p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values.

claim: The age x region interaction in neuronal activation was primarily driven by differences in the anterior cingulate/motor area 2, frontoparietal cortex, and dorsolateral striatum.
source: Simple effect analyses (factor: age) showed that this interaction was primarily driven by differences in the anterior cingulate/motor area 2 (aCg/M2; F(1,14) = 4.912, p<0.05) and the frontoparietal regions of the cortex (FPx: F(1,14) = 15.364, p<0.01), as well as in their target territories of the dorsolateral striatum (DLS: F(1,13) = 4.753, p<0.05) (Ebrahimi et al., 1992; McGeorge and Faull, 1989).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values for specific regions, plus citations supporting anatomical connections.

claim: Sequence length, duration and speed of action could only be predicted by activation in dorsolateral striatum and frontoparietal cortex.
source: We found that sequence length, duration and speed of action displayed on the last day of training could only be predicted by activation in DLS and FPx, whereas activation in all other areas did not significantly correlate with any feature of sequence execution (Figure 4D).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Young mice showed very low levels of correlation overall in regional cross-correlation analysis, with no significant relationships between cortical and striatal territories.
source: Young mice showed very low levels of correlation overall, with no significant relationships between cortical and striatal territories throughout the rostrocaudal extent of the network, perhaps due to automaticity-related reductions in neuronal variability and/or processing loads (Santos et al., 2015; Dayan and Daw, 2008) (Figure 4E, left panel).
evidence: Cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E, with citations supporting the interpretation.

claim: Aged mice showed widespread correlations that were significant in different regions of the corticostriatal network, especially the rostromedial territories.
source: In contrast, aged mice showed widespread correlations that were significant in different regions of the corticostriatal network, especially the rostromedial, but not caudolateral, territories (Figure 4E, right panel).
evidence: Cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Aged mice revealed large regions within the dorsolateral striatum and deep layers of the frontoparietal cortex that were devoid of neuronal activation.
source: Our data in aged mice revealed large regions within the DLS and deep layers of the FPx that were devoid of neuronal activation (Figure 4F).
evidence: Spatial mapping of activated neurons shown in Figure 4F.

claim: hM4Di-mCherry expression was contained within the dorsolateral striatum to eGFP-negative neurons, confirming specific infection of direct pathway spiny projection neurons.
source: We found that hM4Di-mCherry expression was contained, within the DLS, to eGFP-negative neurons, confirming specific infection of dSPNs in the DLS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D confirming cell-type specificity.

claim: dSPN-hM4Di expression and subsequent activation by CNO prevented GBR-induced MAPK phosphorylation compared to the non-injected hemisphere.
source: Importantly, dSPN-hM4Di expression and subsequent activation by CNO prevented GBR-induced MAPK phosphorylation when compared to the non-injected hemisphere of the same animals, ensuring that this system prevents intracellular activation (Figure 5—Figure 1D).
evidence: Comparison of p-MAPK levels between infected and non-infected hemispheres shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Quantification confirmed a pronounced decrease of p-MAPK positive neuron density in infected compared to non-infected hemispheres.
source: Quantification of p-MAPK +neurons confirmed this effect (Figure 5—figure supplement E): paired comparisons revealed a pronounced decrease of p-MAPK +neuron density (t(5) = −15.565, p<0.001) in equivalent areas of infected and noninfected hemispheres (t(5) = −1.222, p=0.276).
evidence: Statistical analysis with t-values and p-values, plus reference to supporting figure.

claim: CNO treatment did not affect the ability of mice to acquire instrumental responses.
source: A two-way mixed ANOVA (factors: training; genotype) showed that the CNO treatment did not affect the ability of mice to acquire instrumental responses, as the rate of LP significantly increased as training progressed in both groups (F(16,192) = 6.389, p<0.001) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to supporting figure.

claim: CNO treatment did not cause a drop in overall performance or detectable behavioral side effects.
source: Importantly, this treatment did not cause a drop in overall performance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, compare days 9 and 10), which equivalently increased in both groups across training (training x genotype interaction: F(16,192) = 0.601, p=0.881). This suggested that 3 mg/kg of systemic CNO did not cause detectable behavioural side effects.
evidence: Statistical analysis and observation from Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: hM4Di(+) littermates tended to display higher sequence rates once CNO treatment started.
source: We found that dSPN-hM4Di(−) and dSPN-hM4Di(+) mice produced a similar number of sequences per minute up to day 9, but hM4Di(+) littermates tended to display higher sequence rates once the CNO treatment started (Figure 5C), as supported by a significant between subjects effect in a two-way mixed ANOVA applied only on CNO days (F(1,12) = 6.380, p=0.27).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-value and p-value, plus reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Both dSPN-hM4Di(−) and dSPN-hM4Di(+) groups showed an equal increase in the number of presses per sequence from day 10 to day 17.
source: Importantly, both groups showed an equal increase in the number of presses per sequence from day 10 (first day of CNO) to day 17 (Figure 5D). Accordingly, a two-way mixed ANOVA showed a significant increase in sequence length in all mice (F(1,12) = 91.036, p<0.001), without a significant day x group interaction (F(1,14) = 19.724, p=0.218).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Only dSPN-hM4Di(−) controls increased the duration of their sequences from day 10 to 17, whereas dSPN-hM4Di(+) littermates displayed the same short latencies throughout.
source: In contrast, we found that only dSPN-hM4Di(−) controls increased the duration of their sequences from day 10 to 17, whereas dSPN-hM4Di(+) littermates displayed the same short latencies throughout (Figure 5E), as supported by a significant day x genotype interaction (F(1,12) = 5.087, p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-value and p-value, plus reference to Figure 5E.

claim: dSPN-hM4Di(+) mice produced overall faster action sequences than controls.
source: We found that dSPN-hM4Di(+) mice produced, overall, faster action sequences (t(12) = −2.3841, p=0.035) (Figure 5F), and also displayed a higher proportion of short IPIs (Figure 5G).
evidence: Statistical analysis with t-value and p-value, plus reference to supporting figures.

claim: dSPN-hM4Di(+) mice displayed significantly shorter average within-sequence inter-press-intervals.
source: Temporal analysis of sequence elements on day 18 revealed that dSPN-hM4Di(+) mice presented a shifted distribution of within-sequence elements in the interval space (Figure 5H) and, consequently, displayed significantly shorter average IPIs (t(12) = 2.964, p=0.012) (Figure 5J), which was a similar trend to that observed in aged mice (see Figure 3J).
evidence: Statistical analysis with t-value and p-value, plus reference to supporting figures.

claim: There were no group differences in the distribution and average value of sequence boundary intervals between dSPN-hM4Di(−) and dSPN-hM4Di(+) mice.
source: However, we found no group differences in the distribution (Figure 5I) and average value (Figure 3K) of sequence boundary intervals (t(12) = 1.435, p=0.177), which was in contrast to the pattern observed in aged mice (see Figure 3K).
evidence: Statistical analysis with t-value and p-value, plus reference to supporting figures.

claim: Interrupting intracellular signaling in direct pathway spiny projection neurons of the dorsolateral striatum during sequence development can increase the speed of individual action sequences.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest that interrupting intracellular signalling in dSPNs of the DLS during periods of sequence development can increase the speed of individual action sequences, although the number of elements fitted within each sequence as well as the extra sequence intervals remained unaltered.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the chemogenetic manipulation results.

claim: The chemogenetic manipulation reproduced within-sequence but not extra-sequence features of action chunking in ageing.
source: Therefore, this manipulation reproduced within-sequence but not extra-sequence features of action chunking in ageing, a pattern that could explain the increased—rather than reduced—ability of dSPN-hM4Di(+) mice to obtain rewards during ST training (t(12) = −2.4, p=0.033) (Figure 5L).
evidence: Comparison of behavioral patterns between chemogenetic manipulation and aged mice, with statistical support.

claim: All aged mice escalated their instrumental responses throughout the duration of the feedback cue experiment.
source: This treatment had no apparent effects on the overall performance of either group: two-way mixed ANOVA (factors: training; cue) showed that all mice escalated their instrumental responses throughout the duration of the experiment (F(35,420) = 72.869, p<0.001), and there was no significant training x cue interaction (F(35,420) = 1.378, p=0.078) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Sequence length dropped significantly from day 18 to day 19 in the Cue Lost group, whereas it remained constant in the Cue Maintained group.
source: Simple effects (factor: day) confirmed that the sequence length dropped significantly from day 18 to day 19 in the Cue Lost group (F(1,8) = 15.696, p<0.01), whereas it remained constant in the Cue Maintained group (F(1,5) = 0.851, p=0.399) (Figure 6C).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values for both groups, plus reference to Figure 6C.

claim: Upon cue removal, the duration of action sequences dropped to pre-sequence levels in the Cue Lost group but not in the Cue Maintained group.
source: This effect was more pronounced on sequence duration: we found significant differences in the duration of the sequences between days 7, 18 and 19 (F(2,26) = 20.643, p<0.001), and again a significant day x cue interaction (F(2,26) = 6.256, p<0.01) with simple effects confirming that, upon cue removal, the duration of action sequences dropped to pre-sequence levels in group Cue Lost (F(1,8) = 21.432, p<0.01) but not in group Cue Maintained (F(1,5) = 0.996, p=0.364) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values for both groups, plus reference to Figure 6D.

claim: The execution of extended action sequences in aged mice depends on the provision of action-related feedback instructing the duration of action.
source: These results suggest that the execution of extended action sequences in aged mice depends on the provision of action-related feedback instructing the duration of action.
evidence: Interpretation of the feedback cue experiment results.

claim: All mice in the Cue Lost group started by executing long action sequences even in the absence of the auditory cue, but these sequences rapidly shortened throughout the session.
source: Event-time diagrams representing the sequences executed at the beginning and at the end of the training session showed that all mice in group Cue Lost started by executing long action sequences even in the absence of the auditory cue, but that these sequences rapidly shortened throughout the session (Figure 6E,F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Observation from event-time diagrams shown in referenced figures.

claim: The length of sequences progressively decreased at the start of the session in the Cue Lost group, but remained constant towards the end.
source: Simple effects analysis (factor: sequence number) revealed that the length of the sequences progressively decreased at the start of the session (F(9,72) = 5.089, p<0.001), but remained constant towards the end (F(9,72) = 0.921, p=0.512) (Figure 6F).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-values and p-values, plus reference to Figure 6F.

claim: The shortening of action sequences precipitated by cue removal was translated into a dramatic increase in the total number of sequences expressed by the Cue Lost mice.
source: Importantly, the shortening of action sequences precipitated by cue removal was translated into a dramatic increase in the total number of sequences expressed by the Cue Lost mice that persisted throughout training (Figure 6G), as indicated by a significant day x cue interaction (F(35,420) = 2.339, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-value and p-value, plus reference to Figure 6G.

claim: Despite the presence of the feedback cue, both groups of aged mice displayed similarly aberrant automaticity on day 10, with boundary intervals accumulating in a narrow band nearby the chunking space.
source: We found that, despite the presence of the feedback cue, both groups of mice displayed similarly aberrant automaticity on day 10, with boundary intervals accumulating in a narrow band nearby the chunking space (Figure 6H, day 10).
evidence: Observation from Figure 6H showing chunking patterns.

claim: Mice seemed to learn to categorize their sequence elements with further cued training as the boundary interval band disappeared in both groups.
source: However, mice seemed to learn to categorise their sequence elements with further cued training as the boundary interval band disappeared in both groups (Figure 6H, Day 18).
evidence: Observation from Figure 6H showing changes in chunking patterns over training.

claim: The Cue Lost group precipitated microchunks as soon as the instructive cue was removed.
source: Strikingly, group Cue Lost precipitated microchunks as soon as the instructive cue was removed (Figure 6H, compare days 18 and 22).
evidence: Observation from Figure 6H showing immediate change in chunking pattern upon cue removal.

claim: Aged mice can execute longer action sequences as long as action-related feedback is provided regarding sequence duration.
source: Taken together, these results show that aged mice can execute longer action sequences as long as action-related feedback is provided regarding sequence duration, suggesting that this deficit is cognitive-motor rather than purely executional in origin.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the feedback cue experiment results.

claim: Motor skill capacity is reduced in older adults, especially in tasks involving fine motor control.
source: Although initial learning capabilities are often preserved (Voelcker-Rehage, 2008; Matamales et al., 2016a), motor skill capacity is reduced in older adults, especially in tasks involving fine motor control.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some studies report that aged humans have a near zero capacity to form action chunks in newly acquired sequences.
source: Indeed, some studies report that aged humans have a near zero capacity to form action chunks in newly acquired sequences (Shea et al., 2006; Verwey, 2010), whereas others find evidence of shortened motor chunks (Bo et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sequence learning appears to be impaired in ageing, although the acquisition of new skills may still be possible through the recruitment of compensatory strategies.
source: Sequence learning appears, therefore, to be impaired in ageing, although the acquisition of new skills may still be possible, perhaps through the recruitment of compensatory strategies (Cabeza et al., 2002; Park and Reuter-Lorenz, 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The precise neuronal mechanism by which advanced ageing affects the acquisition of skills remains unknown.
source: Nevertheless, despite increasing knowledge of the neural bases of action automatisation (Jin and Costa, 2015), the precise neuronal mechanism by which advanced ageing affects the acquisition of skills remains unknown.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field, with citation to relevant work.

claim: Motor skills are generally implemented through sequence learning, which allows elementary action units to be integrated into behavioural streams.
source: Motor skills are generally implemented through sequence learning, which allows elementary action units to be integrated into behavioural streams (Lashley, 1951), reducing latency and increasing speed of action (Sternberg et al., 1978).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Movement sequences are thought to be organised into 'motor chunks', a cognitive-motor strategy proposed to depend on cortico-basal ganglia circuitry.
source: Similar to memory, movement sequences are thought to be organised into 'motor chunks', a cognitive-motor strategy proposed to depend on cortico-basal ganglia circuitry (Graybiel, 1998; Wymbs et al., 2012) that allows expression of whole behavioural programs as a single response (Abrahamse et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement of theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: The development of action sequences and stimulus-response habits is attributed to mediolateral shifts of activity in cortico-basal ganglia circuits.
source: The development of action sequences and stimulus-response habits is attributed to mediolateral shifts of activity in cortico-basal ganglia circuits (Balleine, 2005; Yin et al., 2009; Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010), likely following a medial-to-lateral disposition of functionally relevant corticostriatal projections in rodents (Hunnicutt et al., 2016; Voorn et al., 2004).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Phosphorylated MAPK ERK1/2 is a marker that is widely used to study neuronal activity throughout the brain.
source: We identified over 60,000 activated neurons across cortical and striatal regions in sixteen mice using a confocal imaging-computational approach based on the cyto-nuclear detection and mapping of phosphorylated MAPK ERK1/2 (p-MAPK) (Figure 4A and B), a marker that is widely used to study neuronal activity throughout the brain (Valjent et al., 2004).
evidence: Statement about the marker supported by citation.

claim: Action duration could be influenced by direct pathway spiny projection neurons in the dorsolateral striatum based on their sustained firing during the time of sequence execution.
source: Recent studies have suggested that action duration could be influenced by dSPNs in the DLS based on their sustained firing during the time of sequence execution (Jin et al., 2014), and the prolongation of an ongoing action by optogenetic stimulation (Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Phospho-MAPK is more sensitive in direct pathway spiny projection neurons than indirect pathway spiny projection neurons.
source: Capitalising on our p-MAPK mapping results, and based on findings that this intracellular activity marker is more sensitive in dSPNs than iSPNs (Bertran-Gonzalez et al., 2009), we hypothesised that age-related hypoactivation of dSPNs in the DLS could be contributing, at least in part, to deficits in action sequence learning observed in aged mice.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The use of environmental feedback in the form of action-associated cues has been reported to improve self-initiated performance in older adults.
source: A possible source of the behavioural deficit we observed in aged mice is a loss of action-related feedback; the use of environmental feedback in the form of action-associated cues has been reported to improve self-initiated performance in older adults (Lindenberger and Mayr, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Studies in humans demonstrate that both early and late elderly show very limited use of motor chunking during multi-element sequence tasks.
source: In procedural learning, studies in humans demonstrate that both early (65-68) and late elderly (75-88) show very limited use of motor chunking during multi-element sequence tasks (Shea et al., 2006; Verwey, 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to human studies.

claim: Using a serial response time task in humans, older adults developed motor chunks overall, although the length of those chunks was reduced.
source: Similarly, using a serial response time task in humans, in which the formation of chunks was encouraged using visuospatial cues, Bo et al. (2009) found that older adults developed motor chunks overall, although the length of those chunks was reduced.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Automated or model-free behaviour has advantages for computational and space complexity loads; operationally, model-free reinforcement learning systems require less memory than model-based systems.
source: Over and above the task-efficiency benefits of well-developed skills, automated or model-free behaviour has advantages for computational and space complexity loads; operationally, model-free reinforcement learning systems require less memory than model-based systems (Schneider and Shiffrin, 1977; Dayan and Daw, 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Implementing model-free operations is more appropriate when computational resources such as working memory are limited.
source: One important implication of this is that implementing model-free operations is more appropriate when computational resources such as working memory are limited (Otto et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: The computational resources of the aged brain can be limited by its clearly reduced working memory capacity.
source: On this account, the computational resources of the aged brain can be limited by its clearly reduced working memory capacity (Bo et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011; Wingfield et al., 1988).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Model-based to model-free transition is thought to rely on shifts from dorsomedial to dorsolateral corticostriatal networks.
source: First, model-based to model-free transition (i.e., goal-directed to habitual modes of action) is thought to rely on shifts from dorsomedial to dorsolateral corticostriatal networks (Balleine, 2005; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement of theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: Activity in the frontoparietal cortex and sensorimotor putamen strongly predicts critical features of action sequence execution in humans.
source: Wymbs et al. (2012) found in humans that activity in the frontoparietal cortex and sensorimotor putamen (equivalent to the posterior dorsolateral striatum in rodents) strongly predicts critical features of action sequence execution, and studies in mice have provided information on the specific circuitry within posterior dorsolateral areas involved in action sequence initiation, execution and termination (Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin et al., 2014; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to human and mouse studies.

claim: Several functional imaging studies in humans suggest a shift in activity to anterior regions of the brain in elderly subjects.
source: Indeed, several functional imaging studies in humans suggest a similar shift in activity to anterior regions of the brain in elderly subjects (see Park and Reuter-Lorenz, 2009) for an extensive review): a compensatory overactivation in declining prefrontal cortical regions drives the use of different behavioural strategies to those of younger adults in certain tasks (Cabeza et al., 2002; Gutchess et al., 2005; Raz et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to human imaging studies.

claim: A compensatory overactivation in declining prefrontal cortical regions drives the use of different behavioural strategies to those of younger adults in certain tasks.
source: Indeed, several functional imaging studies in humans suggest a similar shift in activity to anterior regions of the brain in elderly subjects (see Park and Reuter-Lorenz, 2009) for an extensive review): a compensatory overactivation in declining prefrontal cortical regions drives the use of different behavioural strategies to those of younger adults in certain tasks (Cabeza et al., 2002; Gutchess et al., 2005; Raz et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: A large proportion of direct pathway spiny projection neurons recorded in the dorsolateral striatum showed sustained patterns of firing that spanned the duration of an action sequence.
source: Jin et al. (2014) found that a large proportion of dSPNs recorded in the dorsolateral striatum showed sustained patterns of firing that spanned the duration of an action sequence.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of direct pathway spiny projection neurons in the dorsolateral striatum extended the length and duration of ongoing action sequences only during periods of stimulation.
source: More recently, the same group found that optogenetic stimulation of these neurons in the same striatal territory extended the length and duration of ongoing action sequences only during periods of stimulation (Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The ageing brain may engage particular neuronal strategies to automatise action during skill learning.
source: Our findings suggest that the ageing brain may engage particular neuronal strategies to automatise action during skill learning, and that environmental support in the form of action-related feedback can be used to correct this behaviour.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's findings and implications.

claim: Environmental support in the form of action-related feedback can be used to correct aberrant automaticity behavior in aged mice.
source: Our findings suggest that the ageing brain may engage particular neuronal strategies to automatise action during skill learning, and that environmental support in the form of action-related feedback can be used to correct this behaviour.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's findings and implications.

claim: The static properties of aged cortico-basal ganglia networks introduce temporal limits to action automaticity.
source: Our results reveal static properties of aged cortico-basal ganglia networks that introduce temporal limits to action automaticity, something that can compromise procedural learning in ageing.
evidence: Summary statement from the abstract synthesizing the study's main findings.

claim: Static properties of aged cortico-basal ganglia networks can compromise procedural learning in ageing.
source: Our results reveal static properties of aged cortico-basal ganglia networks that introduce temporal limits to action automaticity, something that can compromise procedural learning in ageing.
evidence: Summary statement from the abstract synthesizing the study's main findings.

claim: The stationarity of cortico-basal ganglia transmission is a major feature of the aged brain hampering its ability to acquire new skills.
source: In conclusion, we provide evidence for a severe deficit in corticostriatal function during normal ageing in mice that engenders a distortion of action sequences after extended training. Our findings have implications for skill learning in ageing and point to the stationarity of cortico-basal ganglia transmission as a major feature of the aged brain hampering its ability to acquire new skills.
evidence: Summary statement from the discussion synthesizing the study's main conclusions.

claim: Action-related feedback cues given throughout training transitorily solve the problem of distorted action sequences in aged mice.
source: Importantly, we found that action-related feedback cues given throughout training transitorily solves this problem, a solution that could be readily implemented in current rehabilitation strategies and behavioural therapies for cognitive ageing (Lindenberger and Mayr, 2014).
evidence: Summary statement from the discussion with citation to relevant work on rehabilitation strategies.

claim: Action-related feedback could be readily implemented in current rehabilitation strategies and behavioural therapies for cognitive ageing.
source: Importantly, we found that action-related feedback cues given throughout training transitorily solves this problem, a solution that could be readily implemented in current rehabilitation strategies and behavioural therapies for cognitive ageing (Lindenberger and Mayr, 2014).
evidence: Implication statement with citation to relevant work.

claim: Age-related deficits in corticostriatal activity correlate with the formation of ultrafast oligomeric action chunks in aged mice.
source: We found that, after extended training, aged mice produced shorter actions and displayed squeezed automatic behaviours characterised by ultrafast oligomeric action chunks that correlated with deficient reorganisation of corticostriatal activity.
evidence: The correlation between behavioral features and neural activity patterns is stated in the abstract.

claim: The formation of premature microchunks in aged mice is not a consequence of deficient learning, but rather the result of different automaticity processes put in place by the aged brain.
source: In this case, aged mice expressed long, uninterrupted sequences from the beginning of training, and never displayed the constricted sequences prior to the loss of the cue. These results suggest that the execution of microchunks is not a consequence of deficient learning, but rather the result of different automaticity processes put in place by the aged brain.
evidence: Interpretation of the feedback cue experiment results.

claim: Young and aged brains start from a different neuronal environment or scaffolding and attempt to optimize instrumental task performance by implementing entirely different strategies for automaticity.
source: Rather, our study supports the notion that young and aged brains start from a different neuronal environment or scaffolding (Park and Reuter-Lorenz, 2009), and attempt to optimise instrumental task performance by implementing entirely different strategies for automaticity.
evidence: Interpretation statement with citation to theoretical framework.

claim: The dynamic medial-to-lateral shifts predicted to occur in the corticostriatal network during the development of automatic behaviour may not happen, or may only occur partially, in aged mice.
source: Our data suggest that the dynamic medial-to-lateral shifts that are predicted to occur in the corticostriatal network during the development of automatic behaviour (Yin et al., 2009) may not happen, or may only occur partially, and this neuronal staticity might be key to explaining the recruitment of unusual automaticity processes in aged mice.
evidence: Interpretation of the neuronal mapping results with citation to theoretical framework.

claim: Neuronal staticity in the corticostriatal network might be key to explaining the recruitment of unusual automaticity processes in aged mice.
source: Our data suggest that the dynamic medial-to-lateral shifts that are predicted to occur in the corticostriatal network during the development of automatic behaviour (Yin et al., 2009) may not happen, or may only occur partially, and this neuronal staticity might be key to explaining the recruitment of unusual automaticity processes in aged mice.
evidence: Interpretation of the neuronal mapping results.

claim: The overactivity observed in prefrontal areas in aged individuals reflects failed attempts to boost working memory capacity in distal parietal cortical regions.
source: Again capitalising on age-related working memory deficits and prefrontal cortex dysfunction (Wang et al., 2011; Wingfield et al., 1988), one could speculate that the overactivity observed in prefrontal areas in aged individuals reflects failed attempts to boost working memory capacity in distal parietal cortical regions, following a similar process to that proposed in computational models of visuospatial working memory retention (Edin et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citations to supporting work.

claim: Prefrontal deficits could contribute to the microchunk behavior observed in aged mice.
source: Certainly, these prefrontal deficits could contribute to part of the problem, although the question of how working memory contributes to action organisation remains largely unresolved and is complex, likely involving subcortical basal ganglia circuitry (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citation.

claim: The aged brain may be subject to constraints during the temporal scaling of sequence processing in corticostriatal networks.
source: One interesting possibility is that the aged brain is subject to constraints during the temporal scaling of sequence processing in corticostriatal networks (Fukai, 1999; Igarashi et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citations.

claim: Subcortical networks, particularly the dorsal striatum, are key structures in scaling time for action.
source: Although the precise mechanism by which time is encoded in the brain is unknown, recent evidence clearly implicates subcortical networks (dorsal striatum) as a key structure in scaling time for action (Mello et al., 2015; Soares et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Selectively reducing the activity of direct pathway spiny projection neurons in dorsolateral regions of the striatum reduced action duration while increasing action speed.
source: In our study, we found that selectively reducing the activity of direct pathway spiny projection neurons (dSPNs) in dorsolateral regions of the striatum reduced action duration while increasing action speed.
evidence: Summary of the chemogenetic manipulation results.

claim: The study's results add to studies elucidating the microcircuitry responsible for the temporal scaling of action.
source: Thus, our results add to studies elucidating the microcircuitry responsible for the temporal scaling of action, and suggest the intriguing possibility that the static properties of aged cortico-basal ganglia networks have direct effects on the duration of action sequences, compromising behavioural automaticity.
evidence: Summary statement placing the findings in context of existing literature.

claim: The static properties of aged cortico-basal ganglia networks have direct effects on the duration of action sequences, compromising behavioural automaticity.
source: Thus, our results add to studies elucidating the microcircuitry responsible for the temporal scaling of action, and suggest the intriguing possibility that the static properties of aged cortico-basal ganglia networks have direct effects on the duration of action sequences, compromising behavioural automaticity.
evidence: Interpretive conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Young mice used in the experiments were 2 months old at the beginning of the experiments.
source: Young mice used for the experiments were 2 months old at the beginning of the experiments, whereas aged mice were 20–22 months old.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section.

claim: Aged mice used in the experiments were 20-22 months old.
source: Young mice used for the experiments were 2 months old at the beginning of the experiments, whereas aged mice were 20–22 months old.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section.

claim: The average life expectancy of the mice used in the study is 24 months.
source: We first compared the ability of young (2 months old) and aged (20–22 months old) mice to develop action sequences. We focused on homogeneous sequences involving the concatenation of single responses because this procedure is particularly susceptible to chunking (Garcia-Colera and Semjen, 1987; Jin and Costa, 2015).
evidence: Statement in the results section providing context for the age of the mice.

claim: Homogeneous sequences involving the concatenation of single responses are particularly susceptible to chunking.
source: We focused on homogeneous sequences involving the concatenation of single responses because this procedure is particularly susceptible to chunking (Garcia-Colera and Semjen, 1987; Jin and Costa, 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.
